acceptedAnswer.text: Encapsulation in Java is the OOP principle of bundling data (fields) and the methods that operate on that data into a single unit (class), while hiding the internal state from direct outside access. It is achieved by declaring fields as private and providing public getter and setter methods to read and modify them. Encapsulation protects an object's integrity by ensuring all data modifications go through controlled, validated access points. It answers the question 'HOW is the data stored and protected?' as opposed to abstraction which answers 'WHAT does this do?'.

mainEntity.name: Why do we use private fields in encapsulation?

acceptedAnswer.text: Private fields prevent any outside code from directly reading or modifying an object's internal state. This is critical because: (1) Validation — the setter can check that a value is valid before accepting it (e.g., age cannot be negative). (2) Control — you can make a field read-only by providing only a getter. (3) Flexibility — you can change the internal representation later without breaking any external code. (4) Consistency — invalid states (like a bank account with negative balance) can be prevented at the point of entry. Public fields bypass all of this — anyone can set any value, valid or not.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between encapsulation and abstraction?

acceptedAnswer.text: Encapsulation is about DATA HIDING — protecting internal state using private fields and controlled access via getters/setters. Abstraction is about BEHAVIOUR HIDING — hiding implementation complexity and exposing only essential behaviour through abstract classes and interfaces. Analogy: a capsule medicine — the outer shell (encapsulation) hides the medicine powder inside and controls how it's released; the medicine's effect on your body is the abstraction (you know it cures the disease but not the molecular mechanism). In code: encapsulation = private fields + getters/setters; abstraction = abstract class/interface.

mainEntity.name: What is an immutable class in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: An immutable class is a class whose instances cannot be modified after creation. Every field is final and private, there are no setters, and all mutable fields are defensively copied in the constructor and any getters. Java's String, Integer, LocalDate, and BigDecimal are all immutable. To create an immutable class: (1) declare the class final, (2) make all fields private final, (3) initialize all fields via constructor only, (4) provide no setters, (5) return defensive copies of any mutable field objects in getters. Immutable objects are inherently thread-safe and free of aliasing bugs.

mainEntity.name: What are Java Records and how do they relate to encapsulation?

acceptedAnswer.text: Java Records (introduced in Java 16 as a standard feature) are a concise way to create immutable data-carrier classes with full encapsulation built in. A record automatically generates: private final fields, a canonical constructor, public accessor methods (no 'get' prefix), equals(), hashCode(), and toString(). Syntax: record Point(int x, int y) {} — this single line replaces ~50 lines of traditional encapsulation boilerplate. Records enforce immutability by design — all fields are final and there are no setters. They are ideal for DTOs, value objects, and data transfer between layers.

articleHeader.title: Java Encapsulation — Syntax, Types, Examples & Best Practices
articleHeader.subtitle: Everything you need to know about Java Encapsulation — private fields, getters and setters, data hiding, access modifiers, validation in setters, read-only and write-only fields, immutable classes, defensive copying, Java Records (Java 16+), and real-world production code examples.

blocks.text: Encapsulation is one of the four fundamental pillars of Object-Oriented Programming, alongside Abstraction, Inheritance, and Polymorphism. It is the principle of bundling data (fields) and the methods that operate on that data into a single unit (a class), while hiding the internal state from direct outside access. The word comes from the Latin capsula — a small container — just as a medicine capsule contains and protects its contents from the outside environment.

In real life, encapsulation is everywhere. A medicine capsule hides the powder inside and controls how it is released into the body. An ATM machine hides its cash mechanism — you interact only through the PIN pad and slot, never touching the internal hardware directly. A TV remote encapsulates the circuit board — you press buttons, and the internal signal encoding is hidden. In all these cases, the internal details are protected; you interact only through a defined, controlled interface.

In Java, encapsulation is achieved by: (1) declaring all fields as private — making them inaccessible from outside the class, and (2) providing public getter methods to read those fields and public setter methods to modify them — with validation logic inside the setters to prevent invalid data from ever entering the object.

blocks.title: 🔑 Java Encapsulation at a Glance
blocks.text: Core encapsulation mechanism: (1) private fields — data cannot be accessed or changed directly from outside. (2) public getter — controlled read access: getFieldName(). (3) public setter — controlled write access with validation: setFieldName(value). (4) Read-only field — getter only, no setter. (5) Write-only field — setter only, no getter (rare). (6) Immutable class — all fields final, no setters at all — object state never changes after construction. (7) Java Records (Java 16+) — compiler auto-generates all encapsulation boilerplate.

sections.title: Data Hiding — The Foundation of Encapsulation

blocks.text: Data hiding is the core mechanism of encapsulation — it means making fields private so that no code outside the class can directly read or modify them. Without data hiding, any code anywhere in the project can set a field to an invalid value, creating bugs that are nearly impossible to trace. With data hiding, all access goes through one controlled point — the getter or setter — where you can validate, log, transform, or react to changes.

items.title: Without Data Hiding — Dangerous
With Data Hiding — Safe
Benefits of Data Hiding
items.text:
1. Prevents invalid state — validation at the entry point.
2. Single responsibility — all write logic in one place.
3. Easy debugging — if age is wrong, check setAge().
4. Change-proof — change internal storage without breaking callers.
5. Read-only fields — simply omit the setter.
6. Thread safety foundation — easier to synchronize one method.

sections.title: Getters & Setters — Controlled Access to Private Fields

blocks.text: Getters and setters are the access points of an encapsulated class. A getter (accessor method) reads and returns the value of a private field. A setter (mutator method) accepts a new value, optionally validates it, and assigns it to the private field. Together, they give the class full control over how its data is read and written — now and in the future — without exposing the underlying field.

blocks.label: GettersSetters.java — Naming, Patterns & Advanced Usage

throw new IllegalArgumentException("Salary cannot be negative: " + salary);
throw new IllegalArgumentException("Department cannot be blank");

// ── Conditional setter — applies raise only if eligible ────────

// ── Masked getter — sensitive data partially hidden ────────────

blocks.title: 💡 Boolean Getters Use 'is' Prefix, Not 'get'
blocks.text: Java naming convention and the JavaBean specification require boolean getters to use the 'is' prefix: isActive(), isLoggedIn(), isVerified(), isPremium(). NOT getActive() or getIsLoggedIn(). This convention is respected by all Java frameworks — Spring, Hibernate, Jackson (JSON serialization), and Lombok all look for the 'is' prefix when processing boolean fields. Using 'get' for booleans causes serialization bugs and fails framework auto-discovery.

sections.title: Role of Access Modifiers in Encapsulation

blocks.text: Access modifiers are the language-level enforcers of encapsulation. They control the visibility of classes, fields, methods, and constructors across different scopes — the same class, the same package, subclasses, and the entire codebase. Choosing the right access modifier is not just good style — it is the first line of defence against unintended use of your class internals.

// ── public API — what the outside world sees ──────────────────
public boolean withdraw(double amount, String enteredPin) {

blocks.title: 💡 Principle of Minimum Exposure
blocks.text: Always start with the most restrictive access level and open up only when you have a clear reason: private → default → protected → public. Every unnecessary public or protected member increases the surface area of your API, making it harder to change later. A class that exposes 5 public methods can have its internals freely refactored. A class that exposes 50 public fields has its hands tied — any change risks breaking external code. Professional codebases follow this rule rigorously, and tools like SonarQube flag overly permissive access as code smell.

sections.title: Validation Inside Setters — The First Line of Defence

blocks.text: The real power of encapsulation is not just hiding fields — it is the ability to put validation logic inside setters. Every write to a private field goes through the setter, giving you one central place to enforce business rules, domain constraints, and data integrity. This prevents corrupt object state — a situation where an object holds internally inconsistent data that causes mysterious bugs far from where the bad data was introduced.

blocks.label: ValidationInSetters.java — Product Catalogue
lines: public Product(String sku, String name, double mrp,
double sellingPrice, int stockQuantity, String category) {
"Invalid SKU format. Expected: XXX-0000-XX, got: " + sku);
throw new IllegalArgumentException("Product name cannot be blank");
throw new IllegalArgumentException("Product name too long (max 100 chars)");
throw new IllegalArgumentException("MRP must be positive, got: " + mrp);
// If selling price already set, re-validate it
throw new IllegalStateException("Selling price cannot exceed new MRP");
throw new IllegalArgumentException("Selling price must be positive");
"Selling price (" + sellingPrice + ") cannot exceed MRP (" + mrp + ")");
throw new IllegalArgumentException("Stock quantity cannot be negative");
throw new IllegalArgumentException("Category cannot be blank");
sku, name, mrp, sellingPrice, getDiscountPercent(), stockQuantity, category);

blocks.title: 📌 Call Setters from Constructor — Never Duplicate Validation
blocks.text: Always call your own setters inside the constructor (as shown above) instead of assigning fields directly. This ensures validation runs at object creation time — not just when setters are called later. If you write 'this.name = name' in the constructor, you bypass the null/blank check in setName(). If someone creates a Product with a blank name, the object will be in an invalid state from birth. One validation method, called everywhere — constructor and setter — is always correct.

Encapsulation gives fine-grained control over field access. By selectively providing only a getter or only a setter, you create read-only or write-only fields — enforcing design intent directly in the type system.

blocks.title: 💡 Read-Only vs final — What's the Difference?
blocks.text: A read-only field via encapsulation (private field + getter only) can still be changed internally by the class's own methods (like setStatus() changes status internally). A 'final' field is TRULY immutable — it can only be assigned once, in the constructor or at declaration, and never again. Use 'private final' for fields that should never change after construction (orderId, createdAt). Use 'private' with getter only for fields that the class itself may update but external code should only read (status, balance).

An immutable class is a class whose instances cannot be modified after creation. Every field is set in the constructor and never changed again. There are no setters. Java's own core library is full of immutable classes: String, Integer, Long, BigDecimal, LocalDate, LocalDateTime. Immutable objects are inherently thread-safe, safe to cache, and free from aliasing bugs where one reference unexpectedly modifies another's data.

items.title: Rules for Immutable Class
items.text:
1. Declare class as final — prevents subclass from adding mutable state.
2. All fields private final — cannot be reassigned.
3. No setters — no way to modify after construction.
4. Initialize all fields in constructor.
5. Defensive copy mutable objects passed into constructor.
6. Return defensive copies of mutable fields from getters.
7. If the class has mutable field types (List, Date, arrays), extra care is needed.

items.title: Benefits of Immutability
items.text:
1. Thread safety — safe to share across threads with no synchronization.
2. Caching — safe to cache because state never changes.
3. No defensive copying needed by callers.
4. Simple reasoning — object state is always the same as at creation.
5. Safe map keys & set elements — hashCode() never changes.
6. No aliasing bugs — sharing the reference is safe.

items.title: 'Modification' via New Instances
items.text: Immutable objects don't modify themselves — they return new instances. String example: 'hello'.toUpperCase() returns a NEW String 'HELLO' — the original 'hello' is untouched. Similarly, LocalDate.plusDays(7) returns a new LocalDate — the original is unchanged. This is the standard pattern for immutable 'updates': create a new object with the changed value instead of modifying the existing one.

blocks.label: ImmutableClass.java — Money Value Object
lines: public final class Money {   // 'final' — cannot be subclassed
private final BigDecimal amount;   // 'final' — cannot be reassigned
// Constructor — only place state is set
throw new IllegalArgumentException("Amount cannot be null");
throw new IllegalArgumentException("Currency cannot be blank");
throw new IllegalArgumentException("Amount cannot be negative");
throw new IllegalArgumentException("Result cannot be negative");
if (factor < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Factor cannot be negative");
// ── equals, hashCode, toString — essential for value objects ──
if (!(o instanceof Money m)) return false;
public int hashCode() { return Objects.hash(amount, currency); }
public String toString() { return currency + " " + amount.toPlainString(); }
// 'price' is still unchanged — immutability guarantees this

sections.title: Defensive Copying — Protecting Mutable Internal State

blocks.text: Defensive copying is the practice of making a copy of a mutable object when accepting it into a class (in the constructor or setter) and when returning it from a class (in a getter). Without it, an encapsulated field that holds a mutable reference can be modified from outside the class through the shared reference, completely bypassing all encapsulation. This is one of the most subtle and dangerous encapsulation bugs in Java.

blocks.label: DefensiveCopying.java
lines: // ── BAD: No defensive copying — encapsulation broken ─────────────
this.students = students; // ❌ stores the SAME reference
return students; // ❌ returns the SAME reference
// list.add("HACKER");   // ❌ modifies the roster's internal list!
// roster.getStudents().clear(); // ❌ wipes the roster from outside!
throw new IllegalArgumentException("Students list cannot be null");
// ✅ Defensive copy IN constructor — caller's list changes don't affect us
throw new IllegalArgumentException("Student name cannot be blank");
// ✅ Defensive copy OUT of getter — caller cannot modify our list
// ── Date fields — classic defensive copy need ─────────────────────
private final Date   eventDate;  // Date is mutable!
this.eventDate = new Date(eventDate.getTime()); // ✅ defensive copy IN
return new Date(eventDate.getTime()); // ✅ defensive copy OUT
// Caller modifying returned Date won't affect our field
// ✅ BETTER: Use java.time.LocalDate — it's immutable, no copying needed
original.add("Attacker"); // modifying original — should NOT affect roster

blocks.title: ⚠️ Prefer java.time Over java.util.Date
blocks.text: java.util.Date is mutable and considered legacy. If you use it as a field, you MUST defensively copy it in both constructor and getter. The modern replacement — java.time.LocalDate, LocalDateTime, Instant, ZonedDateTime — are all immutable. With immutable types, defensive copying is unnecessary: no reference to an immutable object can be used to modify it. Prefer java.time types in all new code to eliminate an entire category of defensive-copy bugs.

sections.title: Java Records — Modern Encapsulation Without Boilerplate

blocks.text: Java 16 introduced Records (JEP 395) as a standard feature — a concise, compiler-supported way to create immutable data-carrier classes with full encapsulation built in. A single record declaration replaces the entire boilerplate of: private final fields, a canonical constructor, public accessor methods, equals(), hashCode(), and toString(). Records are ideal for DTOs, value objects, API response models, and any class that simply carries data.

blocks.label: JavaRecords.java — Records vs Traditional Class
lines: // ── Traditional immutable class — ~50 lines of boilerplate ───────
public PointTraditional(int x, int y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; }
if (!(o instanceof PointTraditional p)) return false;
@Override public int hashCode() { return java.util.Objects.hash(x, y); }
@Override public String toString() { return "Point[x=" + x + ", y=" + y + "]"; }
// ── Java 16+ Record — same thing in 1 line ────────────────────────
// Compiler auto-generates: private final fields, canonical constructor,
// public accessors x() and y(), equals(), hashCode(), toString()
record Product(String name, double price, int stock) {
// Compact constructor — no parameter list, fields assigned automatically
throw new IllegalArgumentException("Name cannot be blank");
throw new IllegalArgumentException("Price must be positive");
throw new IllegalArgumentException("Stock cannot be negative");
name = name.trim(); // can reassign parameters before they become fields
public String displayPrice()   { return "₹" + String.format("%.2f", price); }
record UserDto(String username, String email, String role) {}
record ApiResponse<T>(boolean success, String message, T data) {

blocks.text: Encapsulation and abstraction are frequently confused — even by experienced developers. Both are OOP pillars and both involve hiding something, but they hide fundamentally different things and are implemented with different mechanisms.

rows: Internal DATA / state of an object
HOW is data stored and protected?
Protect object integrity — prevent invalid state
The class itself — its own data is protected
The caller — doesn't need to know implementation
Medicine capsule — hides and protects the powder
Car accelerator — hides the engine complexity
Yes — encapsulation without abstraction is common
Yes — abstract class with no private fields

blocks.title: 📌 They Work Together, But Are Not the Same
blocks.text: A well-designed class typically uses BOTH. Example: BankAccount has private fields (encapsulation — hides balance, pin) AND implements an interface like Account (abstraction — hides which bank type it is). Encapsulation protects data inside the class; abstraction hides the class's implementation from its callers. They are complementary, not the same thing.

sections.title: Common Mistakes & Pitfalls — Bugs That Fool Everyone

blocks.text: These mistakes are consistently found in Java beginner and intermediate code involving encapsulation. Each one either breaks data protection or creates subtle state corruption bugs.

blocks.label: EncapsulationMistakes.java
lines: // ❌ MISTAKE 1: Public fields — no encapsulation at all
public String name;   // ❌ anyone can set null, blank, or anything
public int    age;    // ❌ anyone can set -5, -999, no validation
// ❌ MISTAKE 2: Bypassing validation in constructor (not calling setters)
this.name = name; // ❌ bypasses setName() validation — null accepted
this.age  = age;  // ❌ bypasses setAge() validation — negative accepted
if (age < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Age cannot be negative");
// Fix: call setName(name) and setAge(age) in the constructor
// ❌ MISTAKE 3: Returning mutable internal reference from getter
public List<String> getItems() { return items; } // ❌ exposes internal list
// cart.getItems().clear(); // ❌ wipes internal list bypassing all logic!
// ❌ MISTAKE 4: Storing mutable object reference without defensive copy
this.date = date; // ❌ caller keeps reference — can mutate the date!
// d.setTime(0); // ❌ modifies the internal date of 'e' from outside!
// Fix: this.date = new Date(date.getTime()); // defensive copy
public int[] getValues() { return values; } // ❌ returns reference to internal array
// c.getValues()[0] = 999; // ❌ modifies internal array from outside!
// ❌ MISTAKE 6: Setting boolean field name with 'get' instead of 'is'
public boolean getActive() { return active; } // ❌ wrong naming convention
// Fix: public boolean isActive() { return active; }
// Jackson, Hibernate, Spring all look for 'is' prefix for boolean fields

sections.title: Bad Practices & Anti-Patterns — What Senior Developers Reject

blocks.text: These encapsulation anti-patterns are the most common reasons for failed code reviews in professional Java teams. Each either breaks data integrity, creates hidden coupling, or makes the codebase fragile under change.

items.title: Anemic Domain Model
items.text: A class with only getters and setters and zero business logic — all logic lives in service classes that manipulate the model externally. Example: BankAccount with just getBalance()/setBalance() — and a separate BankService that calls account.setBalance(account.getBalance() - amount). This violates OOP — the account should know how to withdraw(). Push business logic into the class that owns the data. An object should protect its own invariants.

items.title: Generating Setters for All Fields Blindly
items.text: IDEs offer 'Generate All Setters' with one click. Using this blindly creates setters for fields that should never be externally modified — like orderId, createdAt, or status. Each unnecessary setter is a hole in your encapsulation. Generate setters ONLY for fields that genuinely need external modification. Question every setter: 'Should external code really be able to change this directly?'

items.title: Protected Fields in Non-Abstract Classes
items.text: Making fields 'protected' in a concrete class so subclasses can access them directly creates tight coupling between parent and child classes. If the parent later needs to change the field name, type, or storage strategy, all subclasses break. Use private fields in the parent and protected getter/setter methods if subclasses genuinely need access. Fields should be private; method access can be protected.

items.title: Setters That Return void in Fluent APIs
items.text: Traditional void setters break method chaining in builder-style APIs. If your class is used with builder-style code, have setters return 'this' to enable fluent chaining: account.setName('Ravi').setSalary(50000). For pure data classes, Java Records or the Builder pattern are better. Mixing traditional void setters with a fluent API expectation is a design inconsistency that confuses users.

items.title: Exposing Internal Collection Without Unmodifiable Wrapper
items.text: Returning a raw internal List, Set, or Map from a getter without wrapping it gives callers the ability to add, remove, or clear elements, bypassing all business logic. Always return Collections.unmodifiableList(), Set.copyOf(), or Map.copyOf(). Even better for true safety, return a defensive copy with new ArrayList<>(items). The choice depends on whether you want callers to see later modifications to your internal list.

items.title: Mutable Static Fields as Shared State
items.text: public static int userCount = 0 with no synchronization and direct public access is the worst of both worlds — global mutable state that any class can corrupt. If you need shared mutable state (like a counter), encapsulate it: private static int count with a synchronized public static void increment() and public static int getCount(). Or use AtomicInteger for thread-safe counters without manual synchronization.

sections.title: Java Encapsulation Interview Questions — Beginner to Advanced

blocks.text: These questions are consistently asked in Java fresher and experienced interviews, OCPJP certification exams, and campus placement tests.

items.q: Q1. What is encapsulation in Java? Why is it important?
items.a: Encapsulation is the OOP principle of bundling data (fields) and the methods operating on that data into one unit (class), while restricting direct access to the fields using the private modifier. Importance: (1) Data integrity — all writes go through setters with validation, preventing invalid state. (2) Flexibility — the internal representation can change without affecting callers (you can change 'private int age' to 'private LocalDate birthDate' and update just the getter — all callers see the same int). (3) Debugging — if 'age' is wrong, check setAge() — there's only one place. (4) Security — sensitive fields like PIN, password hash are never exposed. (5) Controlled API — expose only what external code needs.

items.q: Q2. What is the difference between encapsulation and abstraction?
items.a: Encapsulation = DATA hiding — protecting the internal state of an object using private fields + public getters/setters. It answers HOW the data is stored and protected. Abstraction = BEHAVIOUR hiding — hiding implementation complexity and exposing only essential behaviour through abstract classes and interfaces. It answers WHAT something does. Analogy: a bank ATM — encapsulation hides the cash inside the machine (you can't reach in and take cash directly — you use the PIN pad and slot). Abstraction hides how the machine processes transactions (you don't know if it uses HDFC or ICICI backend systems).

items.q: Q3. What is data hiding in Java? How is it achieved?
items.a: Data hiding means making an object's internal fields inaccessible to external code, so they can only be read or modified through controlled methods. In Java, it is achieved with the private access modifier on fields. With private fields, direct access (object.field = value) causes a compile error — all access must go through public getters and setters. Data hiding is the primary mechanism of encapsulation — encapsulation is the principle, private fields are the implementation.

items.q: Q4. Can we achieve encapsulation without using getters and setters?
items.a: Yes — encapsulation's core is private fields. Getters and setters are the common access mechanism, but they are not the only one. Alternatives: (1) Business methods — instead of 'setBalance(newBalance)', expose 'deposit(amount)' and 'withdraw(amount)' — these are encapsulated operations, not raw field accessors. (2) Immutable classes — no setters at all; all fields are private final. (3) Java Records — auto-generate accessor methods without the 'get' prefix. The key principle is that external code cannot directly set the field — how it accesses it is secondary.

items.q: Q5. What is an immutable class in Java? How do you create one?
items.a: An immutable class produces objects whose state cannot be changed after construction. Creating one: (1) Declare the class final — prevents subclasses from adding mutable state. (2) Make all fields private final — cannot be reassigned. (3) Provide no setters. (4) Initialize all fields in the constructor. (5) Defensively copy mutable objects in the constructor. (6) Return defensive copies (or use immutable types) in getters. Java examples: String, Integer, BigDecimal, LocalDate, LocalDateTime. Benefits: thread-safe without synchronization, safe to cache, no aliasing bugs.

items.q: Q6. What is defensive copying and when is it needed?
items.a: Defensive copying is creating a copy of a mutable object (a) when receiving it into a class and (b) when returning it from a class, so the internal state cannot be modified through shared references. It is needed whenever a field holds a reference to a mutable type — java.util.Date, arrays (int[]), List, Map, Set. Without it: a caller passes a List, stores the reference, then adds items to the original List — the class's field is now modified! Similarly, returning the internal List directly lets callers call .clear() on it. Fix: 'this.items = new ArrayList<>(items)' in constructor; 'return Collections.unmodifiableList(items)' in getter.

items.q: Q7. What are Java Records and how do they relate to encapsulation?
items.a: Java Records (standard from Java 16) are compiler-supported immutable data-carrier classes. A single line 'record Point(int x, int y) {}' generates: private final fields, a canonical constructor, public accessor methods x() and y(), plus correct equals(), hashCode(), and toString(). Records provide encapsulation by design — all fields are private and final, there are no setters, and accessors are generated. They are ideal for DTOs, value objects, and query result carriers. Compact constructors allow adding validation without losing the conciseness benefit.

items.q: Q8. Why should boolean getters use 'is' prefix instead of 'get'?
items.a: The JavaBean specification defines that boolean property accessors must use the 'is' prefix — isActive(), isLoggedIn(), isVerified(). Frameworks that rely on reflection and JavaBean conventions — including Jackson (JSON), Hibernate, Spring MVC, and Lombok — look for 'is' prefix when processing boolean fields. Using getActive() for a boolean field causes: (1) Jackson serializes the field as 'active' from getActive() but looks for a different name. (2) Hibernate may fail to detect the property. (3) Spring form binding may not match correctly. It's also cleaner English — 'if (user.isActive())' reads naturally; 'if (user.getActive())' does not.

items.q: Q9. What is the Anemic Domain Model anti-pattern and how does it violate encapsulation?
items.a: The Anemic Domain Model (term coined by Martin Fowler) is a pattern where domain classes (like BankAccount, Order) contain only fields and getters/setters, with zero business logic — all logic is in separate service classes. Example: BankService calls account.setBalance(account.getBalance() - amount) instead of account.withdraw(amount). This violates encapsulation because: (1) Any service can set the balance to any value — no validation enforced by the object itself. (2) The object cannot protect its own invariants (e.g., 'balance must never go below minimum'). (3) Business logic is scattered in services instead of being co-located with the data it operates on.

items.q: Q10. How does encapsulation help with future code changes?
items.a: Encapsulation creates a stable public API behind which internal implementation can change freely. Example: suppose you store age as 'private int age' today. Later you need to support both 'age' and 'birthDate'. You can change the internal storage to 'private LocalDate birthDate' and update the getter to compute age: 'return Period.between(birthDate, LocalDate.now()).getYears()'. All callers continue calling getAge() and see no change. Without encapsulation ('public int age'), all code that directly accesses the field would break immediately — potentially thousands of call sites. Encapsulation is the foundation of the Open/Closed Principle.

sections.title: Practice Questions — Test Your Encapsulation Knowledge

blocks.text: Challenge yourself with these practice questions. Attempt each independently before reading the answer — active recall is proven to be 2–3x more effective than passive reading.

items.a: Violations: (1) All fields are public — any code can set name = null, gpa = -5 or 999, rollNumber = negative. No validation possible. Fixes: (1) Make all fields private. (2) Add a constructor that accepts all values and calls setters. (3) Add getters for all fields. (4) Add setters with validation: setName() — reject null/blank; setRollNumber() — reject ≤ 0; setGpa() — reject outside 0.0–10.0 range. (5) Boolean getter should be isActive(), not getActive(). (6) Optionally make rollNumber read-only (getter only, no setter) if roll numbers never change after assignment.

Output: 0. Even though Team has a private List, getMembers() returns the direct internal reference. The caller gets that reference, calls clear() on it, and the team's internal list is now empty — completely bypassing the Team class. This is a defensive copy violation. Fix: return Collections.unmodifiableList(members) — caller can read but not modify. Or return new ArrayList<>(members) if you want the caller to have an independent copy. The UnsupportedOperationException thrown by unmodifiableList is preferable to silent state corruption.

Two breaks: (1) Constructor stores the passed-in array reference directly — the caller can later do 'bounds[0] = -999' and modify the internal state of the Range object. Fix: this.bounds = Arrays.copyOf(bounds, bounds.length). (2) getBounds() returns the internal array reference — caller can do 'range.getBounds()[0] = 0' to modify it. Fix: return Arrays.copyOf(bounds, bounds.length). Fixed class: final class Range { private final int[] bounds; public Range(int[] bounds) { this.bounds = Arrays.copyOf(bounds, bounds.length); } public int[] getBounds() { return Arrays.copyOf(bounds, bounds.length); } }

Two immutability failures: (1) Constructor stores the passed list directly — List<String> ext = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Ravi")); Department d = new Department("IT", ext); ext.add("Hacker"); — now d.getEmployees() shows 'Hacker'. Fix: this.employees = List.copyOf(employees) (returns an unmodifiable copy). (2) getEmployees() returns the direct reference — d.getEmployees().add("Hacker") modifies the internal list. Fix: the List.copyOf() in the constructor already returns an unmodifiable list, so the getter can return it safely. Full fix: this.employees = List.copyOf(employees); and getEmployees() can return employees directly since it's already unmodifiable.

Output: HELLO, Hello. String is immutable — toUpperCase() does NOT modify the existing String. It creates a NEW String object ('HELLO') and assigns it to s1. The variable s2 still points to the original String object 'Hello', which is completely unchanged. This is exactly the behavior of immutable objects: 'modifications' return new instances, the original is always preserved. This is why String is safe to pass around — no one can change it through a reference. It also explains why String concatenation in loops is inefficient — each '+' creates a new String object.

items.q: 8. Design an encapsulated Temperature class that: stores temperature internally as Celsius, accepts input in Celsius, Fahrenheit, or Kelvin via static factory methods, provides getters for all three scales, and prevents temperatures below absolute zero (−273.15°C).

sections.title: Conclusion — Encapsulation: The Guardian of Object Integrity

blocks.text: Encapsulation is the guardian of your objects. It ensures that no matter how many places in the codebase create or use an object, the object's internal state is always valid — because every write goes through a controlled, validated entry point. Without encapsulation, a class is just a data bag that anyone can corrupt. With encapsulation, a class is a self-protecting, self-consistent unit of logic.

The difference between junior and senior Java developers is visible in how they approach field access. Junior code uses public fields for convenience. Senior code uses private fields, validated setters, read-only fields where appropriate, immutable classes for value objects, defensive copies for mutable references, and Java Records for clean, boilerplate-free immutable data carriers. These are not style preferences — they are the foundation of bug-free, maintainable, testable Java code.

items.q: What is encapsulation in Java?
items.a: Encapsulation in Java is the OOP principle of bundling an object's data (fields) and the methods that operate on that data into a single class, while hiding the internal state from direct outside access. It is implemented using private fields and public getter/setter methods. Every write to a private field goes through a setter where validation logic prevents invalid data from entering the object. It answers 'HOW is data stored and protected?' — as opposed to abstraction which answers 'WHAT does this do?'.

items.q: Why do we use private fields in encapsulation?
items.a: Private fields prevent any code outside the class from directly reading or modifying the object's internal state. Without private fields, any code can set a field to an invalid value (negative age, null name) with no way to prevent it. With private fields, all writes go through setters where you validate, transform, and control what values are accepted. This guarantees the object is always in a valid, consistent state — no matter how or where it is used.

items.q: What is the difference between encapsulation and abstraction?
items.a: Encapsulation is about DATA hiding — protecting the internal state using private fields and controlled access methods. It answers HOW data is stored and protected. Abstraction is about BEHAVIOUR hiding — hiding implementation complexity and exposing only essential behaviour via abstract classes and interfaces. It answers WHAT something does. Analogy: a medicine capsule — the shell (encapsulation) protects the powder; the medicine's healing effect on the body (abstraction) hides the molecular mechanism.

items.q: What is an immutable class in Java?
items.a: An immutable class produces objects that cannot be modified after creation. All fields are private final, there are no setters, the class is declared final, and defensive copies are made of any mutable fields. Java's String, Integer, BigDecimal, and java.time classes are all immutable. Benefits: inherently thread-safe, safe to cache and share, free from aliasing bugs. To 'modify' an immutable object, you create a new instance with the updated value — the original is unchanged.

items.q: What are Java Records and how do they relate to encapsulation?
items.a: Java Records (standard since Java 16) are a concise, compiler-supported mechanism for creating immutable data-carrier classes with full encapsulation built in. A single line 'record Point(int x, int y) {}' generates: private final fields, a canonical constructor, public accessor methods x() and y(), and correct equals(), hashCode(), toString(). Records enforce encapsulation by design — all fields are final, there are no setters, and all access is through the generated accessors. Compact constructors allow adding validation without losing conciseness.
